text:
The open-source Grok Bot alternative: an AI coworker that acts on its own. It reads every channel, email and event you give it, decides what matters, does the work on its own computer, and speaks up when it should. Demo · Compare · Quick start · How it decides · How it works ⭐ If Pots is useful to you, a star helps other people find it. Tip Setting this up with an AI agent, such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor? Have it read docs/for-agents.md first. That page explains Pots to your agent and how to set it up. In short: the agent installs it and makes the bot, you sign in to your model with pots login , and then the bot connects Slack and your other apps itself. Grok Bot, dots and Claude Tag showed what an AI teammate can be. pi-durable-bot gives you the same kind of coworker as open source: it runs on your machine, with the model you choose, in the places your team already talks. Grok Bot, OpenAI dots, Claude Duet, Claude Tag and Meta Muse are closed products. They run on someone else's computer, with someone else's model, inside the apps they chose. pi-durable-bot is MIT-licensed and runs where you put it. The other products as their makers described them in public, November 2026; they may have changed since. Grok Bot, dots, Claude Duet, Claude Tag and Muse are products of xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta. pi-durable-bot is not affiliated with any of them. Any model. Log in once with a subscription you already pay for, use an API key from any of the 40+ providers pi supports, point it at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (vLLM, SGLang, a proxy), or run a local model with Ollama, LM Studio or llama.cpp. The bot uses pi's own model layer, so every model pi can use, the bot can use. With a local model for the agent and the judge, nothing leaves your machine. You are not locked to one model vendor. Any channel. The core speaks in five plain words: channel, place, thread, message, person. Platform details stay inside one adapter per platform. Slack, Discord and Telegram work today; Teams or email is one more adapter, not a rewrite. One bot can be in many channels and stays the same person everywhere. Your business. Give it your own tools, data and workflows. It can run several bots on one machine, each with its own name, persona, responsibilities and memory. A bot can even edit its own definition, or create a new bot. Most AI bots are a command line with a chat bubble. You @ them, they answer, they forget. A real coworker works differently: Every message in every place you invite it to lands in one inbox: channel messages that never mention it, edits, deletions, reactions, people joining, and its own messages. It keeps all of it in a local SQLite log and reads that log with SQL whenever it needs context. Nothing is thrown away when a conversation gets long. It is woken in three ways, the same three ways a person notices work: Being woken is not the same as speaking. Each time, the agent reads the log and decides if it should say anything, where, and when. Most of the time the right answer is to stay quiet. It has a real machine with a shell, files, the internet, and a screen it uses like a person: the browser and the apps on it, with the mouse and keyboard. It does not wait for a plugin. It writes the script it needs, runs it, fixes it, and keeps the useful ones. That covers research, spreadsheets, reports, monitoring a web page, filling a form, or booking a flight, and also code. This is code mode : the agent gets a few general tools ( read , write , edit , bash , screen ) plus three channel actions ( send , react , call ), and builds the rest itself. One more tool, task , hands work to its helpers (below). With codemode , pi's code mode, it writes a JavaScript script that calls these tools and the tools of MCP servers in a sandbox; only what the script returns comes back to it. screen is bash with the screen's environment, such as DISPLAY ; bash does not have it. A screen runs one task at a time, as a person's desktop does: the first screen command of an agent takes the screen until its work ends, also across bots and the Pots processes of the same user on the machine. Another agent that tries then learns who has it, since when, and when it frees, and decides itself what to do. A bot that sets up its own desktop, such as an Xvfb display, writes its environment into screen in its bot.json . One agent at a time per screen is enforced only on Linux, where plain bash has no DISPLAY or WAYLAND_DISPLAY and so cannot reach the screen. On macOS and Windows the screen does not depend on those variables, so bash can still use it; there the agents use the screen tool because the prompt tells them to. Longer work does not keep it from talking. With its task tool the bot starts children : agents that work in the background with read , write , edit , bash , screen and codemode , without the channel actions and task , on a brief it writes for them. It answers the person first, hands the work to a child, and stays free for the next message. A child starts from an empty conversation and its brief, so the bot's own context stays small; it sees the bot's memory index as it was when it started. When a child ends, done, failed or with a question for a person, its final message comes back to the bot as a wake, exactly once, also across crashes and restarts; the bot passes on what matters, and sends the child the answer to its question. While a child works for a place, new messages there go to the bot, so it can pass them on. Its timed and fallback wakes list the children that work and how long each has run. A stopped child reports nothing and does nothing more, also when the process dies in the middle of the stop. Children use the bot's model, or the childModel of bot.json ; a change counts for new children and those that exist, also when childModel is taken out. The bot chooses each child's thinking level when it starts it: high , xhigh or max , and without a choice the childThinking of bot.json ( xhigh by default). A child keeps its level for its whole life, so a new childThinking counts for new children only; a level the model does not have becomes the nearest one it has, as in pi. settings.maxChildren (50 by default) caps how many work at once. pots children lists them, and pots children --stop or --stop-all stops them. It works like a pi session: it reads AGENTS.md and uses Agent Skills from the same places pi does, so the skills you give pi, the bot can use too. Screenshots and photos are shrunk to fit the model, as in pi. When it speaks, it speaks like a teammate: in the right channel or thread, in its own words, with the file attached. It can reply in a thread, start a new message, DM a person, add a reaction, edit its own message, or call any other platform API. Some things do not fit in a chat message. For a plan, a report or a dashboard, the bot writes a web page and sends a link. A page can ask, too: people choose, comment, fill in, approve or reject on it, and each answer wakes the bot at once. It promises to come back, and it does. A timed wake ( pots wake ) wakes it once, at a time it chooses. A routine ( pots routine ) repeats: every 30 minutes, say, or on a cron schedule in the computer's time zone. Both live in the same database as everything else, so they survive restarts. It can also add normal cron jobs on its machine. Each bot has one long conversation, across every channel. Its memory works as Claude Code's automatic memory: plain markdown files, one per memory, and an index, MEMORY.md , that the bot sees at the start of every page and that points to them. The bot saves what is worth keeping (preferences, rules, facts about people and the work, decisions) when it sees it, and after each piece of work its own model, continuing the same conversation in the background, saves what it missed. That pass never sends a message or holds up a reply, its request starts as the bot's last one did, so the provider's prompt cache serves most of it, and code lets it change nothing but the memory. Once a day, after enough changes, a dream tidies the memory up the same way. The bot's next wake says what a pass or a dream changed; as in Claude Code, a restart before that wake loses the note, not the memory. A memory file read two days or more after it changed says how old it is. Each bot has its own memory, in memory/ in its folder, and the bots of one computer share one more, in ~/.pots/memory/ , for facts about you. "Remember this" and "forget that" work by talking to it; to forget is to delete the file, as in Claude Code. "settings": {"autoMemory": false} in bot.json turns the memory off. When the context gets full, the bot decides when to turn the page : it writes notes for itself, starts a fresh context, and the notes and the memory come with it. The full message log stays on disk, so nothing is lost. Its AGENTS.md , its responsibilities and its notes are plain files it edits itself. Built on pi-durable , every step is journaled. Kill the process in the middle of a task and it continues after restart. Every incoming event is written to disk before it is acknowledged. Every outgoing message carries a send ID, and after a crash the bot checks whether the message already went out before it sends again. Important The bot gets full control of the computer it runs on, with no approval step. Give it a computer or VM of its own. You need Node.js 24 or newer, on macOS, Linux or Windows (with Git for Windows ). npm install -g pi-durable-bot pots init pots init asks four things: Then the gateway starts as a background service (it starts again at login) and you are talking to your bot in the terminal. It first checks that it can use the computer's screen and walks you through any permission it needs, such as Screen Recording and Accessibility on a Mac. On a server with no desktop, it works without a screen and asks you before it sets one up. Tell it which chat apps to join. It sets them up itself on its computer and asks you only for what it cannot do, like signing in to Slack or approving the app. Leave with Ctrl+C; come back with pots chat . It joins only the places it is invited to, like a new hire who is added to the right channels. To upgrade, run npm install -g pi-durable-bot@latest , then pots service restart . To remove it, run pots service uninstall , then npm uninstall -g pi-durable-bot . The bots stay in ~/.pots/ until you delete that folder. pots init sets up the model, and pots login signs in to another one or adds a key, for every bot on the computer. Each bot's bot.json names its model and, if you want one, a judge, and you can change them at any time; edits apply within seconds. Logins, API keys and local endpoints are stored in pi's files in ~/.pi/agent/ , so the pi command line, if you use it, shares them. With off , each group of messages is a wake of the main model, which then decides. A fast classifier keeps the messages that are not for the bot away from it, and is cheaper and quicker than the main model: Jev answers in about 0.3 seconds. With main , each group of messages costs one short request to the main model before the bot hears of it. OpenAI-compatible and local endpoints (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, a proxy): pots init and pots login add them for you. By hand, they go in pi's ~/.pi/agent/models.json ( fields ): { "providers" : { "ollama" : { "baseUrl" : " http://localhost:11434/v1 " , "api" : " openai-completions " , "apiKey" : " ollama " , "compat" : { "supportsDeveloperRole" : false , "supportsReasoningEffort" : false }, "models" : [{ "id" : " qwen3:8b " , "contextWindow" : 32768 }] } } } Then set "model": "ollama/qwen3:8b" . The agent needs a model that calls tools well and a context window of 32K tokens or more. In our tests a 4B model judged well but was too small to do the work alone; use the largest model your machine runs well. llama.cpp can be both the agent and the judge. Start llama-server in router mode, then log in once with the pi command line: run pi , then /login llama.cpp ( guide ). Its chat models appear as llama.cpp/ . For the judge, use a decision model such as Kev-4B (3 GB), which answers through llama.cpp's /v1/systemone ; any chat model also works as a judge. { "model" : " llama.cpp/ " , "judge" : " llama.cpp/Kev-4B-Q4_K_M " } MCP servers The bot uses MCP servers through pi's own MCP support. They are set in pi's files: ~/.pi/agent/mcp.json for every bot on the computer and the pi command line, and .pi/mcp.json in a bot's workspace/ for that bot alone. The bot's codemode scripts call their tools, as with pi's default exposure, so the tools the model is told about never change and the provider's prompt cache keeps serving; a section of the prompt lists the servers. A server added, removed or changed applies from the bot's next wake, with no restart. pots mcp is pi's pi mcp , with the same options ( pots mcp --help ); npm links only pots , so pi may not be on your PATH. Sign-ins are stored in pi's ~/.pi/agent/mcp-auth.json , and the bot uses a new one from its next request. When the browser is on another computer, as over SSH, paste the address the browser was sent to into the terminal. The bot also looks for a command line tool, an API or an MCP server before it uses the screen. When it finds a command line tool that has no skill yet, it offers to write one in ~/.agents/skills/ , so every bot and pi know when and how to use it. flowchart LR E[New event] --> L[(Message log)] E --> M{Mention or DM?} M -- yes --> W[Wake the agent] M -- no --> J{Judge, if set:

Other messages that arrive close together are grouped: it waits 3 seconds after the last one (20 seconds at most) before it decides. If it is already working in a place, itself or with a child, new messages there are handed to it as it works, so it can change course. The wake message says where, who, why and when, and gives each new message's text, the start of its thread when it is a reply, and its files. The gateway downloads files as soon as a message comes, into the bot's files/tmp/ , so the wake gives their paths on the machine; it deletes them 30 days later, and the log keeps each file's name, type, size and URL, so the bot can download it again. A file over 10 MB is not downloaded, and a download that passes 10 MB, when the channel gave no size, stops and is deleted; the wake waits for the other downloads at most 10 seconds past the moment it would go out without them; for a file that is not saved, it gives the URL, and the bot downloads it itself if it needs it. Earlier messages and other details are in the log. Translates events in and actions out, backfills what it missed. Platform concepts never leave this layer. Gateway core Inbox, message log, waker and outbox. The same for every platform. Bot Identity, persona, responsibilities, notes, timers, workspace and one long conversation. Agent pi-durable : runs the model, journals every step, owns the tools. One gateway process runs every bot on the machine. Everything lives in ~/.pots/ (or $POTS_HOME ): one folder per bot in bots/ , channel tokens in secrets/ , the memory the bots share about you in memory/ , the gateway's output in logs/ on macOS and Windows (on Linux, pots service logs reads the journal). Each bot folder holds: The same pots command gives the bot (and its scripts and cron jobs) its actions from a shell: pots send , pots react , pots call , pots wake , pots routine , pots context , pots turn-page , pots children . Tokens stay inside the running gateway; the agent never sees them. The bot sends its whole conversation with each model request, so the provider's prompt cache matters: a request whose start the provider has cached costs a fraction. The system prompt holds only facts that stay the same, and the bot's own parts of it, its memory too, keep their text for the whole page; a change, such as a new settings value in bot.json , shows after the page turns, after pi compacts, or after an upgrade. What changes from one wake to the next, such as the time, the context use and the bot's own address in a channel, is in the wake. pots trace and pots context show how much of the input the cache served and what the requests that missed it cost. pi-durable-bot runs every day as a teammate in a real workspace. What works today and what is next: git clone https://github.com/Crokily/pi-durable-bot && cd pi-durable-bot npm install npm run pots -- status # the pots command, straight from src/ (Node 24 runs TypeScript) npm run check # type check npm test # tests, including a real gateway with a fake model npm run tla # the TLA+ models of the inbox, outbox and waker (needs Java and tla2tools.jar) npm run build writes the JavaScript that the npm package ships to dist/ . Set POTS_HOME to try things without touching ~/.pots/ . With OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT set, the gateway also sends its traces to any OpenTelemetry tool (Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Honeycomb). Tests, the TLA+ models and traces in detail: docs/development.md . Coding agents: read AGENTS.md . Agents that set Pots up for someone: read docs/for-agents.md . MIT. The demo video, music, sky images and logo in docs/media were made for this project and use the same license.
